detailed_rationale:
Sai Life Sciences is an integrated CRDMO (contract research, development and manufacturing organization) serving global innovator pharma/biotech clients across the drug lifecycle, from early discovery through commercial-scale manufacturing. The growth numbers are genuinely strong: revenue_growth_1y of 29.2% and a 3-year CAGR of 21.7%, with the latest reported quarter (Q4 FY26, Mar 2026) at Rs 602cr sales, Rs 104cr PAT and 29% OPM - a clear step up from Q1 FY26's Rs 496cr / Rs 60cr / 24% OPM base. This fits the broader 'China+1' CDMO outsourcing tailwind, where global pharma/biotech innovators are diversifying manufacturing and development partners away from Chinese CDMOs, a structural trend that benefits credible Indian players like Sai with established Western-innovator relationships.

The quality picture is more mixed than the growth headline suggests. Live ROE (15.4%) and ROCE (19.6%) are healthier than the quant sheet's own stale figures (7.9%/15.9%), but even the live 3-year average ROE (12.7% per screener) is unexciting for a company trading at ~80x earnings and ~11.5x book. More concretely, working capital has deteriorated sharply - receivable/working-capital days have moved from 12 to 78 days, and debtor days sit at an elevated 62 - a real, quantifiable red flag that needs to be watched closely: it could reflect the normal cash-conversion lag of scaling up manufacturing-stage CDMO contracts (larger, longer-cycle commercial-manufacturing work naturally carries more inventory and receivables than early-stage discovery work), or it could signal collection or execution slippage. The company does not pay a dividend, which is unremarkable for a still-scaling, capital-intensive CDMO reinvesting in capacity.

Ownership: promoter/founder holding has drifted only modestly (35.23% to 34.53% since Dec 2024), consistent with a relatively recently-listed company (IPO December 2024) where post-listing float dynamics are still settling. No adverse USFDA plant-status news (483s, warning letters, OAI) was found in available reporting, which is a mild positive but not a confirmed clean bill of health given how recently the company has been public.
recommendation_rationale: Quant recommendation is Hold on both windows. The structural CDMO growth story and recent quarter's execution are real enough that a Sell would be wrong, but the rich valuation (~80x earnings, ~11.5x book) against only a mid-teens live ROE and a genuinely deteriorating working-capital profile (12 to 78 days) means this isn't priced as a bargain either - Hold is the honest middle ground until the working-capital trend either normalizes or is explained.
summary: Sai Life Sciences is a contract research, development and manufacturing partner to global pharma and biotech companies, benefiting from the industry-wide shift of manufacturing and development work away from Chinese suppliers. Growth has been strong and margins are improving, but the stock is priced richly (around 80x earnings) and working capital has deteriorated noticeably in recent quarters - receivable and inventory days have risen sharply - which is worth watching before treating the growth story as fully de-risked. We rate it a Hold.
positive_para: Sai Life Sciences sits at the center of a real structural tailwind - global innovator pharma and biotech companies diversifying CDMO relationships away from China - and the numbers back up the thesis: 29% trailing revenue growth, operating margin stepping up from 24% to 29% between recent quarters, and a long-standing base of Western-innovator client relationships that are hard to replicate quickly. This is a genuine growth business in a structurally advantaged position, not a story built on hope alone.
negative_para: The working-capital deterioration is the number that deserves the most scrutiny here - receivable/working-capital days moving from 12 to 78, with debtor days at 62, is a material shift, not a rounding error, and at minimum it means the company's cash conversion is far less efficient today than it was recently. Layered on top of a rich ~80x earnings, ~11.5x book valuation and a 3-year average ROE of only 12.7%, the stock isn't being given much room for that working-capital trend to be anything other than temporary - if it reflects actual execution or collection strain rather than a benign mix-shift toward longer-cycle commercial manufacturing contracts, the current multiple would be difficult to defend.
reverse_dcf_judgment: At ~80x trailing earnings and ~11.5x book against a 3-year average ROE of only ~12.7%, the market is pricing several more years of high-double-digit revenue growth and continued margin expansion for a CDMO that has been public for barely two years - a demanding but not unreasonable ask given the sector tailwind, provided the recent working-capital deterioration proves temporary. This is a growth-priced-for-perfection valuation rather than a comfortably cheap one; it needs sustained execution, not just a good structural narrative, to be earned back.
